sugestoes.texto: WHAT: When Storage.Create fails, the code records a legacy-duration metric instead of a storage-duration metric. WHY: This corrupts the dual_writer_legacy_duration_seconds histogram with values from the unified store and makes the storage-error path invisible in the storage metric. HOW: Replace `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)` in the error branch.

WHAT: When Storage.Update fails, the code records a legacy-duration metric instead of a storage-duration metric. WHY: It misattributes the unified-store error to the legacy store and leaves the storage-duration histogram without an error observation. HOW: Replace `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)` in the error branch.

WHAT: The async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records a storage-duration metric for the legacy call. WHY: It puts legacy-call latency into the dual_writer_storage_duration_seconds histogram and leaves the legacy histogram without an observation. HOW: Use `d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` inside the goroutine.

WHAT: On successful Delete, the storage-duration metric is observed with `name` as the third label instead of `options.Kind`. WHY: The third histogram label is `kind`; passing the object name creates inconsistent label values across methods and inflates metric cardinality with unique names. HOW: Pass `options.Kind` to match the error path and other methods.

WHAT: The goroutines spawned for async legacy writes are created from the request context using `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`. WHY: The request context is canceled when the HTTP handler returns, so the async legacy write is likely canceled before it completes, defeating mode 3's purpose of writing to legacy as a safety measure. HOW: Detach the goroutine context from request cancellation, e.g. `context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), time.Second*10, ...)` so it can run to completion or its own timeout.

WHAT: Every Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection spawns a new goroutine that can live up to 10 seconds with no concurrency limit or backpressure. WHY: Under high write throughput this creates unbounded goroutine fanout and memory growth, especially if the legacy store is slow or times out. HOW: Bound concurrency with a worker pool or semaphore, or use a rate-limited background queue for legacy writes.

The test file constructs a single shared *mock.Mock and embeds it in both legacyStoreMock and storageMock, which define separate mock methods over the same underlying mock object. Because both d.Storage.Create and d.Legacy.Create route through that single shared Mock, expectations are matched against whichever method name the concrete type invokes. This works only because the mock instance is shared, so the test is fragile and relies on that shared-instance coupling rather than on distinct, independent mocks.

Inconsistent metric recording in the production DualWriterMode3 code: recordStorageDuration is used versus recordLegacyDuration, and options.Kind/name are used inconsistently (for example, the Delete success path records name instead of options.Kind). This is a single-hunk issue rather than a cross-file disagreement, but the labels/names recorded are inconsistent.

In Delete, `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` is computed but never used. The next line does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, so the enriched `log` is discarded and context logs lose the name/kind/method tags. It should use `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` like the other methods.

When `d.Storage.Create` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. It should call `recordStorageDuration` because the failure came from Storage, not Legacy. As written, the storage error path is credited to the legacy metric with the storage start time.

When `d.Storage.Update` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. It should call `recordStorageDuration`, matching the Delete path. The storage failure is currently attributed to Legacy.

After a successful Storage Delete, the code records `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. All other metric calls in this file use `options.Kind` as the resource/kind label. This mismatch will break queries/dashboards that group by kind. It should use `options.Kind` to stay consistent with the error path and other methods.

The success case 'deleting an object in the unified store' only configures a mock for Storage.Delete and asserts only the synchronous result. The implementation also spawns a goroutine that calls Legacy.Delete, but the test exits immediately. If the legacy write were removed from the implementation, this test would still pass. Worse, because no expectation is registered for Legacy.Delete, the test can panic if the goroutine runs before the test returns, making it flaky.

The success case 'deleting a collection in the unified store' only mocks Storage.DeleteCollection. The implementation spawns a goroutine that also calls Legacy.DeleteCollection, but the test does not register that expectation and returns before the goroutine completes. This means the test passes even if the legacy collection deletion is removed, and it may panic on a slow run when the unmocked legacy call executes.

The success case is named 'creating an object only in the unified store', but the implementation also writes to LegacyStorage in a goroutine. The test registers a Legacy.Create mock but never asserts it is called, so the test would still pass if the legacy write were entirely removed. The test name should match the actual dual-write behaviour and the test should verify the legacy call is attempted, or use a synchronization primitive to wait for the goroutine.

Update passes the same `objInfo` to `d.Storage.Update` synchronously and then to `d.Legacy.Update` in a goroutine. Because `rest.UpdatedObjectInfo` may hold mutable state and `UpdatedObject` can produce different results when invoked at different times or against different stored objects, Storage and Legacy may apply different versions of the update, violating the dual-write consistency invariant and creating a data race. The previous code pre-computed the updated object and wrapped it for both stores; that synchronization should be preserved or a copy/thread-safe wrapper should be used.

At line 45, when `d.Storage.Create` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. This records the storage failure under the legacy duration/error metric, corrupting the metric labels. It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`.

At line 129, when `d.Storage.Update` returns an error, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`. The failure is in Storage, not Legacy, so it should be recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)`.

At line 166, the goroutine performing `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` calls `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. Because the operation is on LegacyStorage, it should call `d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)`.

The test case 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' still sets up a Legacy.Create mock expectation, but the new DualWriterMode3.Create contract (lines 42-46) returns immediately when Storage.Create fails and never calls Legacy.Create. Update this test to match the new contract: remove the Legacy expectation in the storage-failure path and assert that Legacy.Create is not invoked. If the intent is to verify the new async path, add synchronization so the goroutine is observed before assertions.

issues.descricao: Delete puts the base d.Log instead of the enriched per-call logger into the context, so downstream logs lose name/kind/method fields.
issues.textoGolden: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

comentarios.texto: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` installs the mode-level logger instead of the request-scoped `log` built on line 96 (which carries name, kind and method) — a copy/paste error, as every other method in this file passes the composed `log`. Storage.Delete and the legacy delete goroutine therefore log without the per-request fields this PR is adding (and without the metrics method/kind context).
ctx is built with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of the enriched `log`. The delete logs then lose the name, kind and method values. Use `log`.
The Delete context uses d.Log rather than the per-call log. This is a logging-context inconsistency (not a data leak); use the per-call logger for consistency.

issues.descricao: The legacy DeleteCollection goroutine records its duration with recordStorageDuration instead of recordLegacyDuration, misattributing legacy latency and errors to the storage metric.
issues.textoGolden: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

comentarios.texto: The legacy DeleteCollection duration and error status are recorded in the unified-storage histogram. Every successful unified deletion therefore produces a second storage observation for a different backend, while legacy deletion failures are attributed to unified storage and no legacy observation is emitted. Call recordLegacyDuration here instead.

The timed call is d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, but its measurement is emitted using recordStorageDuration. Use recordLegacyDuration; otherwise storage receives two measurements for a successful collection deletion and legacy receives none, and legacy failures appear as storage failures.
The legacy DeleteCollection duration is recorded with recordStorageDuration, so legacy latency and errors are attributed to storage. Use recordLegacyDuration.

issues.descricao: Delete's success path records the storage metric with the object name in the kind label instead of options.Kind, creating per-object series and inconsistent labels.
issues.textoGolden: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

comentarios.texto: The Delete success-path metric passes `name` where every other call site in this file (lines 48, 103, 113, 156, 159) passes options.Kind in the kind/name argument slot. The storage-success sample for Delete is thus labelled with the object name instead of the resource kind, breaking label consistency with the other operations and with the error sample emitted at line 103. Use options.Kind here (or insert name consistently everywhere, matching the metric's label semantics).
recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) at line 106 passes the object name in the kind label slot.

recordStorageDuration is called with the object `name` as the `kind` label: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)`. Every other storage call site passes `options.Kind` (lines 73, 89, 103, 156, 159). This injects a per-object value into the kind label, corrupting the metric and giving it unbounded cardinality (one series per object name), which grows memory on every delete. Should be `options.Kind`.

issues.descricao: On storage Create/Update failure the duration is recorded with recordLegacyDuration, attributing unified-store errors to the legacy metric.

comentarios.texto: On a Storage.Create failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) — the failing subsystem is Storage, not Legacy, and it passes the storage start time. This records storage failures under the legacy metric, corrupting the dual-writer error dashboards (and contradicts the success path on line 48 which uses recordStorageDuration). Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

On a Storage.Update failure the code records the error with recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), attributing a storage failure and its storage duration to the legacy metric. This is inconsistent with the success path on line 132 (recordStorageDuration) and with mode1's semantics. Use d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

The async goroutine performing the LEGACY DeleteCollection measures it with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). Every other legacy write in this file uses recordLegacyDuration (lines 56, 113, 140); recording it under the storage metric reports legacy latency/errors as storage latency/errors. Use d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy).

issues.descricao: Mode 3 legacy writes now run in background goroutines derived from the request context, which is cancelled when the request completes, so legacy writes can be cancelled and legacy storage falls out of sync.

comentarios.texto: The async legacy write goroutine derives its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)). The apiserver cancels that context as soon as the HTTP handler returns — which is immediately after Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection return — so the goroutine's Legacy.Create can be canceled before completing, silently dropping the legacy write that this mode exists to guarantee. The same applies to the goroutines at lines 108-114, 134-141 and 161-167. Detach the async context from request cancellation (e.g. derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) / context.Background()) before applying the timeout.

The legacy write in Mode 3 became fire-and-forget, changing the contract callers relied on: previously Create (and, identically, Update/Delete/DeleteCollection) returned only after the LegacyStorage call had been made in-request; now it returns immediately and the write runs in a detached goroutine. Worse, the goroutine builds its context from the request-scoped `ctx` (line 51: `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`), which the API server cancels as soon as the handler returns/flushes the response — so the legacy write and its 10s timeout will typically be cancelled outright and the legacy store silently stops being updated, which is precisely what the new mode-3 integration cases assume still happens. Any detached work must be given a context not tied to the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a server-lifetime context), and consumers that depended on the synchronous legacy write need to be updated.

The asynchronous legacy write derives its timeout context from the request context, which is canceled when the HTTP request finishes. Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection return before this work completes, so their legacy database operations can be canceled immediately instead of receiving the intended ten-second window. Derive the bounded background context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) to retain request values without inheriting request cancellation.

issues.descricao: Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo instead of a wrapper carrying the object stored in unified storage, so legacy recomputes the update and can diverge.

comentarios.texto: Legacy.Update receives the original objInfo instead of the object successfully committed to unified storage. The playlist legacy implementation calls objInfo.UpdatedObject(ctx, old) against its own legacy object, so a patch is reapplied to potentially stale state and can persist a different result or fail rather than mirror the unified write. Pass an updateWrapper containing res, as the previous implementation did.

Legacy.Update previously received an updateWrapper containing the object returned by Storage.Update; it now receives the original objInfo. UpdatedObjectInfo can compute an update from the old object supplied by each backend (notably for patches), so evaluating it against a stale legacy object can produce a different result or reject an update that already succeeded in Storage. Preserve the canonical-result contract by passing an updateWrapper with updated: res and upstream: objInfo to the legacy consumer rather than replaying the original update against legacy state.

Legacy.Update now receives the original objInfo rather than the updateWrapper containing the object successfully committed to Storage. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a patch/transform based on the supplied old object; replaying it against legacy's potentially different old state can persist a different result or fail, even though the authoritative update succeeded. Restore forwarding of the committed result via updateWrapper instead of recomputing the update against legacy state.

issues.descricao: The Mode 3 tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes, and legacy and storage share one mock, so removing the legacy calls would not fail them.

comentarios.texto: The legacy half of Mode 3 is never verified, so these tests cannot catch its removal. Mode 3 is documented as writing to BOTH LegacyStorage and Storage, and the implementation performs the legacy write in a detached goroutine (`go func(){ d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`, dualwriter_mode3.go lines 50-57, and likewise at 108-114, 134-141, 161-167). Each test registers legacy expectations (`setupLegacyFn`, e.g. lines 30-32 and 40-42) but never calls `m.AssertExpectations(t)`, `AssertCalled` or `AssertNumberOfCalls`, and never waits for or observes the goroutine — no channel, no polling. Additionally `legacyStoreMock{m, l}` and `storageMock{m, s}` (lines 53-54, and the same pair in every other test function) share one `*mock.Mock`, so even a count assertion could not distinguish a legacy call from a storage call. Deleting every `d.Legacy.*` call from the implementation leaves all six tests passing, which is exactly the regression the names — and the Mode 3 contract — claim to cover.

The successful Create test never verifies the legacy write. Configuring m.On("Create", ...) does not require that expectation to be consumed, and these assertions only inspect the object returned by Storage.Create. Deleting the entire legacy-create goroutine would still pass this test. Use distinct storage and legacy mocks and synchronize on the legacy call, then assert that it completed with the intended object.

The successful Update case configures a legacy Update expectation but returns after checking only the unified-store result. It neither waits for the asynchronous legacy update nor verifies its expectation, so removing the legacy-update goroutine entirely still passes. Add explicit synchronization and verification of the legacy update (ideally with separate mocks), including the object propagated to legacy storage.

issues.descricao: The List error test case is still named 'not implemented' although List is now implemented and the case checks storage error propagation.

comentarios.texto: The test-case name "error when listing an object in the unified store is not implemented" still describes the old stub List (which returned nil, nil with a "List not implemented" log). List is now implemented at dualwriter_mode3.go:79 and delegates to Storage.List; the case merely checks that a Storage error is propagated. The name contradicts the code it now exercises — rename it, e.g. "error when listing objects in the unified store fails".

issues.descricao: The Create test case name says 'only in the unified store' although Mode 3 also writes to legacy.

comentarios.texto: The test name says creation happens "only in the unified store", but this case configures a successful Legacy.Create as well, and Mode3.Create launches that legacy write after the unified write succeeds. Rename the case to describe creation in both stores (with the legacy write asynchronous), so test output does not communicate the opposite of the mode-3 write contract.

issues.descricao: Independent per-request goroutines remove ordering between legacy writes to the same resource, so legacy can end up with an older version or a resurrected object.

comentarios.texto: Independent goroutines remove ordering between successful writes to the same resource. For example, Storage commits update A and then update B, but the legacy goroutine for B can finish before A, leaving legacy with A while Storage contains B. Likewise a delete can run before an earlier create and leave a resurrected legacy object. Preserve per-resource commit order for mirroring (including across create/update/delete), rather than launching each write independently.

issues.descricao: The storage-failure Create test registers its failing expectation via setupLegacyFn and only works because legacy and storage share one mock.

comentarios.texto: The 'error when creating object in the unified store fails' case registers the failing Create expectation only through setupLegacyFn. It passes only because legacy and storage share one mock, so the storage Create gets that error by accident. Register the expectation in setupStorageFn and use separate mocks for legacy and storage, so the test really covers a storage failure.

issues.descricao: DualWriterMode3.Delete now returns on any unified-storage error, including NotFound, before deleting from legacy, so objects that exist only in legacy can no longer be deleted.
Mode 3 legacy-storage write errors (create/update/delete/delete-collection) are no longer logged after moving to async goroutines; only a duration metric with an error flag is recorded.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The call to SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId passes an empty data object, which Prisma treats as a no-op. WHY: With data: {}, Prisma performs no actual column writes, so the @updatedAt timestamp on SelectedCalendar is not refreshed and the cache-status UI continues to show a stale 'last updated' time. HOW: Pass { updatedAt: new Date() } in the data argument so the timestamp is explicitly updated.

WHAT: connectedCalendarsHandler directly constructs CalendarCacheRepository instead of using the CalendarCache.init factory. WHY: The factory checks the 'calendar-cache' feature flag globally and returns a no-op mock when disabled; bypassing it forces a calendarCache.groupBy query on every settings-page load even for tenants that have the feature turned off. HOW: Use CalendarCache.init(null) (or await the feature check) to obtain the repository so the mock is used when the feature is disabled.
Only sends credential IDs and static i18n keys; no raw errors or PII are logged or displayed. Cache timestamps shown belong to the user's own credential. No data-exposure issue found.
Exposes only credentialId + latest cache updatedAt, used solely to enrich the caller's own connected-calendars response. No data-exposure issue found.
Changes are DB-only with no logging; updateManyByCredentialId is called with empty data. No data-exposure issue found.
Returns a generic "Credential not found or access denied" error, which does not leak existence or details. No data-exposure issue found.
Echoes and logs the public tunnelmole webhook receiver URL; that URL is intended to be public and is not a secret credential or PII-bearing value. No data-exposure issue found.

The new updateManyByCredentialId method passes `data` directly to `prisma.selectedCalendar.updateMany`. Its caller in CalendarService.ts invokes it with `{}` to bump `updatedAt`, but Prisma's updateMany requires at least one field in `data`; an empty object causes a Prisma Client validation error and breaks the availability refresh. Either pass `{ updatedAt: new Date() }` from the caller, or make the repository method always include `updatedAt: new Date()` internally when the caller wants to touch the timestamp.

The code calls `SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` to update `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt`, but an empty `data` object does not change any columns and therefore will not trigger Prisma's `@updatedAt` (and may throw). Pass `{ updatedAt: new Date() }` (or another real change) so the timestamp is actually updated.

The caller intends to touch `updatedAt` for every `SelectedCalendar` row belonging to the credential, but it passes an empty `{}` update object. Prisma's `updateMany` needs at least one field in `data`; with an empty object it will either throw a validation error or issue no UPDATE, so `updatedAt` is not refreshed. Pass `{ updatedAt: new Date() }` (or another field) so the update is valid and the timestamp is actually updated.

issues.descricao: fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId with an empty data object, so Prisma does not refresh the @updatedAt timestamp and SelectedCalendar.updatedAt never reflects the cache refresh.
issues.textoGolden: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: updateManyByCredentialId is called with empty data {} to bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. WHY: Prisma updateMany rejects empty data (validation error) or no-ops without touching @updatedAt, so the refresh path throws or silently leaves updatedAt stale. HOW: pass an explicit touch field e.g. { updatedAt: new Date() }.

Comment claims "Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt" but call passes empty object {} as data, so nothing is updated (Prisma updateMany with empty data is a no-op/error). Fix comment or pass { updatedAt: new Date() } to match the stated intent.

updateManyByCredentialId is called with empty data {}. Prisma updateMany throws when data is empty, so this line throws on every resync after the cache write. Pass an explicit touch e.g. { updatedAt: new Date() } instead of {}.

issues.descricao: After deleting the calendar cache, CredentialActionsDropdown does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, so where no parent refetch callback is passed the stale cache status and delete action remain visible.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `deleteCacheMutation`'s `onSuccess` only calls `onSuccess?.()` and never invalidates the `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query, while the sibling `disconnectMutation` explicitly invalidates it in `onSettled`. WHY: the 'Cache Status' row in the dropdown is rendered from the cached `connectedCalendars` result; after deleting the cache the query is not refetched, so the deleted status/last-updated entry stays visible and stale in the UI. HOW: invalidate the query in the cache-deletion mutation as well, e.g. `const utils = trpc.useUtils(); onSuccess: async () => { ...; await utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate(); }`.

WHAT: deleteCacheMutation onSuccess only calls onSuccess?.() and never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, unlike disconnectMutation onSettled. WHY: cacheUpdatedAt stays stale after deletion so UI keeps showing old Last updated and delete action until manual refetch. HOW: add onSettled invalidate of connectedCalendars like disconnect does.

Successful cache deletion does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query that supplies cacheUpdatedAt. The wrapper forwards only an optional parent onChanged callback and disables window-focus refetch, so the deleted cache continues to appear present with its old timestamp and delete action. Invalidate utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars on successful deletion.

issues.descricao: The cache 'last updated' timestamp is formatted with a hard-coded en-US locale instead of the user's locale, so non-US users see US-style dates in an otherwise translated label.
issues.textoGolden: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

comentarios.texto: The 'Last updated' timestamp is formatted with a hard-coded "en-US" locale (new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)), so every user — regardless of their locale — sees a US-style date/time while the surrounding label is translated. Use the app's locale-aware date formatting helper (the user's current locale) instead of pinning en-US.

Date format hard-coded to "en-US" via Intl.DateTimeFormat while surrounding strings use t()/useLocale. Users in other locales see US short date/time. Use the active locale from useLocale/i18n instead of hard-coding "en-US".

The cache timestamp is always formatted with "en-US", even though the surrounding label uses the user's selected translation locale. Users in other locales therefore see US month/day ordering and time conventions inside an otherwise localized message, potentially misreading the last-update date. Use the active application locale for Intl.DateTimeFormat instead of hard-coding en-US.

issues.descricao: The calendar cache migration keeps a generated warning saying updatedAt has no default and cannot be added to a non-empty table, although the SQL adds it with DEFAULT NOW().

comentarios.texto: This warning says updatedAt is added without a default and cannot be added to a nonempty table, but the migration actually supplies DEFAULT NOW(), explicitly handling existing rows. Remove or correct the warning so operators reviewing the migration are not incorrectly told that existing data makes it unsafe to run.

issues.descricao: The test-gcal-webhooks.sh cleanup function always exits 0, including when called from the failure paths, so the script reports success when the tunnel could not be set up.

comentarios.texto: `cleanup` always runs `exit 0`, and it is also called on the failure paths (rate limit hit, failed to extract the URL). The script therefore reports success even though the tunnel failed and GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL was never updated. Have `cleanup` take an exit code, and pass 1 from the failure paths.

cleanup() always ends in `exit 0`, and both failure paths (rate-limit at lines 46-50 and 'Failed to extract Tunnelmole URL' at lines 56-59) call cleanup. So a script named test-gcal-webhooks that did not actually obtain the tunnel URL / update GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL still exits with status 0, letting any automation treat the run as successful even though the setup it verifies failed. On the failure branches the script should exit non-zero (e.g. `exit 1`) so failure is observable; only the SIGINT/SIGTERM interactive shutdown should exit 0.

issues.descricao: The webhook test script updates .env with the macOS-only `sed -i ''` syntax, which fails on Linux GNU sed and leaves GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL unchanged.
issues.textoGolden: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

comentarios.texto: WHAT: `sed -i '' -E 's|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|...|' "$ENV_FILE"` uses the BSD/macOS `sed -i ''` form. WHY: under GNU sed (typical Linux dev/CI environment) the empty `''` is consumed as the script operand and the command errors, so the existing `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` line is never replaced and the tunnel URL is not written to the env file. HOW: use a portable invocation, e.g. `sed -i.bak -E "s|^GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=.*|GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL=$TUNNEL_URL|" "$ENV_FILE"` (or branch on `uname`).

The environment update uses BSD sed's `-i ''` syntax, which fails with GNU sed on Linux. When GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL already exists, the script leaves the previous URL unchanged but still prints that it was updated, preventing webhooks from reaching the new tunnel. Use a portable replacement strategy or select the in-place syntax based on the available sed implementation and check its exit status.

When GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL already exists, `sed -i ''` uses BSD/macOS syntax and fails under GNU sed on Linux. The script nevertheless prints that the URL was updated and keeps the tunnel running, leaving webhooks configured with the old URL. Use a portable replacement approach (or select the appropriate sed syntax) and only announce success after the edit succeeds.

issues.descricao: deleteCacheHandler throws a plain Error when the credential is missing or not owned by the user, so tRPC returns a 500 instead of a structured FORBIDDEN/NOT_FOUND error.
issues.textoGolden: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

issues.descricao: connectedCalendarsHandler instantiates CalendarCacheRepository directly instead of the feature-flag-aware factory, so cache status is queried and shown even when calendar-cache is disabled.
The dev script writes tunnelmole output to a fixed /tmp/tmole.log, so a local attacker's symlink at that path could make it overwrite an arbitrary file.

sugestoes.texto: WHAT: The SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is true, but `GrafanaRuleListItem` passes only `promRule` and leaves `rule` undefined. WHY: Clicking the Silence action in the Grafana rule list menu sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true but the drawer never mounts, so users cannot silence Grafana rules from the list view. HOW: Also check the prom rule type, e.g. change the condition to `(rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) || prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(promRule)) && showSilenceDrawer`.

WHAT: The `GrafanaRuleListItem` rendered for `origin === 'grafana'` omits the `key` prop, while the `datasource` and `default` branches include `key={key}`. WHY: React will use index-based keys for this list, which can cause component state to be reused for the wrong rule when the filtered list reorders or updates, leading to incorrect actions/links being shown. HOW: Add `key={key}` to `GrafanaRuleListItem`.

WHAT: `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` gates `ModifyExport` on `isAlertingRule`, which is true only for alerting rules, whereas the ruler-based equivalent gated it on `isGrafanaManagedAlertRule` (true for all Grafana-managed rules). sugestoes.texto: WHAT: readInteger accepts constructed INTEGER tags (e.g., 0x22) because it only masks the low 5 bits of the tag byte. WHY: DER/BER requires INTEGER to be primitive; accepting constructed encodings silently parses malformed input as a valid integer, diverging from BouncyCastle's strict parser. HOW: Reject the constructed bit by checking `(tag & ASN1Encoder.CONSTRUCTED) == 0` before reading the value.

WHAT: The ignored-providers log calls `logger.debugf(builder.toString())`, but debugf expects a format string. WHY: A provider class name containing `%` (e.g., from a shaded/proxied jar) would cause `MissingFormatArgumentException` and abort detection; even without that, it is the wrong logging API. HOW: Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` and avoid the trailing comma.

WHAT: getBouncyCastleProvider returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, the JVM's default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider. WHY: This violates the CryptoProvider contract documented to return a BouncyCastle provider and misidentifies the provider in BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER/logs when AuthzClientCryptoProvider is selected. HOW: Return null so BouncyIntegration.loadProvider falls back to the first installed provider, which is the documented null-handling behavior.

WHAT: concatenatedRSToASN1DER creates two ASN1Encoder instances at lines 114-115 and discards them. WHY: This is leftover dead code that allocates and encodes the integers before the real sequence encoding at lines 117-121; it performs no work and is misleading. HOW: Remove the two unused encoder calls.

The test in ECDSAAlgorithmTest.test() only asserts that converting a signature DER -> concatenated RS -> DER -> concatenated RS yields the same concatenated bytes twice. This round-trip assertion cannot detect a broken conversion that corrupts the signature symmetrically. The test should verify the re-encoded DER signature against the original data using Signature.verify() with the public key, or compare rsConcat to a value derived from the original sign, so the test fails if the ASN.1/RS conversion corrupts r or s.

The method name getBouncyCastleProvider() promises a BouncyCastle provider, but the implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which is the platform default keystore provider (usually SUN for JKS). This identifier/code disagreement can mislead callers that rely on BouncyCastle-specific behavior. Either return an actual BouncyCastle provider or rename the method/role to reflect that it provides a generic fallback provider.

The method assumes signature.length == signLength and copies signLength/2 bytes from it. A malformed or mismatched concatenated signature causes an unhandled ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Validate that signature is non-null, signLength is even, and signature.length == signLength before copying, throwing IOException for invalid input.

The method assumes signature.length == signLength. It allocates r/s of size len+1 and copies len bytes from signature without validation; a shorter input causes an out-of-bounds read. Add an explicit check (e.g., if (signature.length != signLength) throw new IOException(...)) before the array copies.

When qLength < bytes.length, the method copies only the lowest qLength bytes. For a malformed or non-minimal DER integer whose value exceeds the curve coordinate size, this silently changes the numeric value instead of rejecting the signature. It should throw if bytes.length > qLength + 1 (after allowing at most one sign-padding zero) or if stripping that zero still leaves more than qLength bytes.

issues.descricao: concatenatedRSToASN1DER encodes r and s into two throwaway ASN1Encoder instances before re-encoding them in the return statement.
issues.textoGolden: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

comentarios.texto: Dead computation: the two ASN1Encoder.create().write(...) calls allocate encoders and encode rBigInteger/sBigInteger, but their results are discarded — the returned DER comes entirely from the expression at lines 117-121, which re-encodes the same BigIntegers. These two statements have no effect and should be removed (they are a leftover from an earlier formulation).

Remove these two discarded encoder writes. Each allocates an encoder and encodes a BigInteger, but neither result participates in the returned signature; lines 119–120 repeat both writes on fresh encoders. This performs redundant encoding and allocations on every concatenated-signature conversion.

The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` encode values and discard the results. The return expression re-encodes the same values, so these lines are dead computation left over from a copy-paste or refactor. Remove them.

issues.descricao: order() is added to CryptoProvider as an abstract method, breaking source and binary compatibility for existing third-party CryptoProvider implementations.
issues.textoGolden: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

comentarios.texto: order() was added as an abstract method to the public CryptoProvider interface. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider now invokes order() on every ServiceLoader-discovered CryptoProvider via Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order). Any CryptoProvider implementation compiled against the previous interface (an external or separately built provider jar on the classpath) will throw AbstractMethodError at detection time, i.e. during AuthzClient.create()/server bootstrap, before any provider is usable. Giving order() a default implementation (e.g. default int order() { return 0; }) avoids the binary-incompatibility.

issues.descricao: detectProvider no longer fails when several crypto providers are present; with Default, FIPS and Elytron all at order 200, ties are resolved by classpath order and a FIPS deployment can silently run with the non-FIPS provider.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: detectProvider sorts by order() reversed and silently picks index 0, removing the previous multiple-providers error. WHY: Default/FIPS/Elytron all return order 200, so ambiguous classpath (e.g. default+FIPS) now nondeterministically picks one by ServiceLoader order instead of failing fast, risking wrong FIPS vs non-FIPS crypto. HOW: only auto-ignore lower-order providers; throw when the top two have equal order().

Reject ambiguous highest-priority providers rather than silently taking the first. Both DefaultCryptoProvider and FIPS1402Provider return order 200 in this PR, so when both are present the stable sort leaves the decision to ServiceLoader discovery order. A deployment expecting FIPS can therefore initialize the ordinary Bouncy Castle provider without an error; previously this mixed classpath failed closed. Preserve the error for tied highest-priority providers (or require an explicit security-mode/provider choice), while still allowing the lower-priority authz-client fallback.

detectProvider() no longer fails fast when multiple CryptoProviders are present and instead silently picks the first after sorting by order() descending. All Keycloak providers return the same order (DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, WildFlyElytronProvider all return 200), so a tie between two providers is broken by the non-deterministic ServiceLoader iteration order rather than the intended priority. The previous code threw an IllegalStateException forcing the classpath to be corrected; now a deployment with two provider jars (exactly the 'multiple providers on classpath' scenario this PR enables) can silently select the unintended provider — e.g. a non-FIPS/strict provider when FIPS is required — with no error. Use a stable tie-breaker (delegate to the provider name/type) or reject equal top orders instead of relying on ServiceLoader order.

issues.descricao: Claims a wrong-length JOSE signature causes an unchecked exception in concatenatedRSToASN1DER; verifiers catch it and report verification failure, as with the existing providers.

comentarios.texto: WHAT: concatenatedRSToASN1DER splits signature without validating signature.length==signLength. WHY: short JOSE input throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and long input is silently truncated to signLength, breaking the ECDSACryptoProvider contract (IOException on malformed) used by verifier contexts. HOW: check length upfront and throw IOException.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER never validates signature.length == signLength before System.arraycopy(signature,0,r,1,len) / (signature,len,s,1,len). A short JWS signature throws unchecked ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of the declared IOException, breaking verification on attacker-controlled input. Validate length and throw IOException.

issues.descricao: The ES384 and ES512 tests sign with the same default P-256 key, so the converter is never tested with real P-384 or P-521 signatures.

comentarios.texto: Single default EC keypair reused for ES256/ES384/ES512: testES384/testES512 names claim larger curves but body signs with the same P-256 key and only pads to larger signLength, so full-width 384/521-bit handling is never exercised. Generate a per-algorithm keypair with the correct curve (e.g. secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) before signing.

Every case generates a default EC key rather than a key on the curve associated with the named algorithm. On the standard JDK this is P-256, so testES384 and testES512 just pad P-256 signature components to larger lengths. A converter that discards nonzero high bytes beyond 32 bytes would still pass all three cases. Initialize the key generator with the appropriate curve per case (P-256, P-384, and P-521) so the larger-component conversions are actually tested.

Generate a key on the curve corresponding to each tested algorithm rather than using the provider's default EC curve for all three tests. On the standard JDK this generates a P-256 key even for testES384 and testES512, so those tests merely pad P-256 integers to larger output lengths and never exercise actual P-384/P-521 signature encoding (including P-521's long-form sequence length).

issues.descricao: The test only checks a round trip between the two new converters and never verifies the re-encoded DER against the original signature or with Signature.verify, so mutually consistent bugs go undetected.

comentarios.texto: Tautological round-trip assertion: rsConcat2 is derived from rsConcat via encode+decode that are inverses if self-consistent, so assertArrayEquals(rsConcat,rsConcat2) passes even if both directions are wrong. Verify against external oracle: Signature.initVerify + verify(asn1Des) and/or compare rsConcat to expected split, not just to itself.

The test only checks self-consistency: it asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(g(asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign))) == asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign), i.e. that concatenatedRSToASN1DER is a right inverse of asn1derToConcatenatedRS. It never compares against the original DER `sign`, never verifies the ECDSA signature, and never asserts the emvider output is canonical DER. Because the decoder it reads back with (ASN1Decoder.readLength) accepts non-canonical long-form lengths (e.g. 0x81) and validates only tag numbers, a regression in ASN1Encoder.writeLength that always emitted long form would still round-trip and the test would still pass, even though the produced signature would no longer be valid DER and would be rejected by the Keycloak server / a JDK Signature.verify. Assert the encoded signature is valid DER (e.g. verify it with a JDK Signature, or compare asn1derToConcatenatedRS(sign) against a known-good width-padded r||s and assert its length equals algorithm.getSignatureLength()).

The assertion only establishes agreement between the two new conversion routines, not correctness of the converted signature. For example, swapping r and s in both routines makes this entire round trip pass, although the DER result no longer verifies the signed data. Verify `asn1Des` with the public key and original data (or compare against an independently specified encoding) so mutually compensating conversion defects fail the test.
